statement: In young adults aged 21 to 24 in a Los Angeles cohort who had drunk alcohol in the past month, having ever used hangover remedy pills (such as dihydromyricetin), compared with never having used them, is associated with more alcohol-related problems and heavier drinking on drinking days: 2.3 points higher on a 0 to 40 problem scale (95% CI 0.8 to 3.8), about a quarter more drinks per drinking day (rate ratio 1.24, 1.02 to 1.49) and almost twice as many symptoms of alcohol use disorder in the past year (rate ratio 1.86, 1.18 to 3.02), but not with more drinking days or binge-drinking days; only 42 of 1312 (3.2%) had ever used such pills, while 18.9% had heard of them and 8.6% believed they work (Han et al., 2024). The survey was cross-sectional, so it cannot say whether the pills lead people to drink more or heavier drinking leads people to try the pills, and it asked only whether people had ever used pills. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Few young adults in one Los Angeles survey had ever used hangover pills (about 3 in 100). Those who had reported more drinking problems and more drinks on the days they drank, but the survey cannot tell whether the pills led to heavier drinking or heavier drinkers tried the pills.
population: 1312 past-month drinkers aged 21 to 24 in a school-based cohort in Los Angeles, surveyed in 2021
exposure: Ever having used hangover remedy pills (for example dihydromyricetin), self-reported
comparator: Past-month drinkers in the same survey who had never used them
outcome: Modified AUDIT problem score; drinks per drinking day; drinking days and binge-drinking days in the past month; count of alcohol-related problems
magnitude: Adjusted for sociodemographic factors and depressive symptoms: modified AUDIT difference 2.29 (95% CI 0.82 to 3.76) on a 0 to 40 scale; drinks per drinking day rate ratio 1.24 (1.02 to 1.49); alcohol-related problems rate ratio 1.86 (1.18 to 3.02), also adjusted for drinking frequency and intensity; drinking days 1.19 (0.94 to 1.51) and binge days 1.40 (0.91 to 2.23), not significant. Prevalence: ever used 3.2% (42 of 1312), heard of 18.9%, believe they work 8.6%.

evidence.extracted: Of 1312 past-month drinkers aged 21 to 24, 42 (3.2%) had ever used hangover remedy pills, 248 (18.9%) had heard of them and 110 (8.6%) believed they work.

evidence.locator: Table 2, Alcohol use problem score, drinks per typical drinking day and Past Year AUD symptom count rows; Results, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The ever-use group scored higher than never-users on the modified AUDIT (7.7 against 5.4; adjusted B = 2.29, 95% CI 0.82 to 3.76), drank more per drinking day (adjusted rate ratio 1.24, 1.02 to 1.49) and reported more past-year alcohol use disorder symptoms (1.7 against 0.9 of 7; adjusted rate ratio 1.86, 1.18 to 3.02, also adjusted for drinking frequency, binge frequency and intensity).

evidence.locator: Table 2, drinking days and binge drinking days rows; Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Ever-use was not detectably associated with drinking days (adjusted rate ratio 1.19, 0.94 to 1.51) or binge-drinking days (1.40, 0.91 to 2.23).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Methods › Measures › Hangover remedy use
evidence.extracted: A single yes-or-no item asked about ever using hangover remedy pills; the authors state that causal interpretation is not possible, that ever-use does not separate recent from past or occasional from regular use, and that the small number who had used pills limits power.

risk_of_bias.note: One crude self-report item for the exposure, self-reported outcomes recoded from ranges, and a school-based cohort with unreported attrition; important confounders (earlier drinking, hangover frequency, sensation seeking) were not adjusted for.

indirectness.note: Worded for ever-use of pills in this cohort.

imprecision.note: Only 42 people had used the pills; intervals for the counts are wide.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, giving very low. The claim is worded as an association; whether remedy pills lead to heavier drinking is a separate causal question that this design cannot answer. The 'AUD symptom count' of the paper is described here as alcohol-related problems, because its items are the AUDIT's problem items rather than diagnostic criteria. Placed in section 7 with the other remedy claims; the editor may prefer section 8. Single study.
